tagline.text: A house of the Virgin in northern Luzon that has called pilgrims for 400 years

children.text: One of the Philippines' largest Marian pilgrimage sites, dating back to the early 17th century — a minor basilica enshrining an ivory image of the Virgin. You can visit the panyalikip where pilgrims touch the Virgin's mantle, the candle gallery, and the rosary garden all on a day trip from Manila.
Manaoag Church, formally the Minor Basilica of Our Lady of the Most Holy Rosary of Manaoag, stands on a hill in the small town of Manaoag in eastern Pangasinan. It's about
200km

north of Manila, and Filipino Catholics know it best as the home of Our Lady of Manaoag. On weekends, pilgrims arrive from across the country by chartered bus and van to have new cars blessed and pray for exams, jobs, and health. It's beloved enough locally that telling a Filipino friend or coworker "I visited Manaoag" is sure to get a warm reaction.
According to legend, around

a farmer walking along the road heard a voice calling him and saw the Virgin Mary, holding a rosary, atop a tree wrapped in clouds. A church was built where she had pointed, and the town's name is said to come from the Pangasinan word for "to call." The image of the Virgin was brought in by the Dominican priest Juan de San Jacinto aboard a Manila galleon via Acapulco, Mexico — a 17th-century ivory-and-silver statue of the Virgin and Child.
The site's history began with a small chapel built by the Augustinians in

, which soon passed to the Dominicans, who still care for the church today. The building burned during the 1898 revolution, but the image survived unharmed, and a bomb that fell during World War II without exploding is also remembered as a miracle. The present church was rebuilt between
. The image was canonically crowned with papal approval on
April 21, 1926
, and in
February 2015
Pope Francis officially declared the church a Minor Basilica.

It's a pilgrimage site well worth a visit for any Catholic, and even for non-believers it offers a close look at Filipino faith and daily life. The church itself can be seen in an hour or two, making it a popular stop on the way to Hundred Islands, Baguio, or the beaches of La Union.
Mass is held several times a day, starting at
6 AM
on weekdays and
5 AM
on Sundays. Most are said in English, Tagalog, or Pangasinan, and you can pray while looking at the image of the Virgin enshrined behind bulletproof glass above the altar.

Climb the stairs beside the church to a small room behind the altar, where you can reach through a small window to touch the Virgin's mantle in prayer. It's the signature ritual of a Manaoag pilgrimage, and the line runs long on weekends, so allow plenty of time.

A candle-offering area behind the church, where thousands of candles burn around a statue of the Virgin set above a pond. Each candle color is tied to a particular intention — health, peace, wealth — and pilgrims traditionally buy the color that matches their prayer.

blocks.title: Blessing of religious items and vehicles

children.text: After every Mass, priests bless religious items such as rosaries and statues, as well as vehicles. Many Filipinos come here to have a new car blessed, so the blessing area is always crowded with vehicles on weekends.

A small museum housing crowns, halos, scepters, and vestments offered to the Virgin, along with replicas of old images of her. The dim, quiet lighting makes it a calm place to take in 400 years of religious history.

A garden of statues depicting the mysteries of the rosary, pleasant to walk through while meditating. Unlike the crowded church interior, it's relatively quiet, making it a good spot to rest for a while.

blocks.title: Browse the street in front of the church

children.text: The streets around the church are lined with shops selling rosaries, statues, and candles, along with stalls selling Pangasinan snacks. Try local treats like tupig, a rice cake, and Calasiao puto, and pick some up as gifts.
Board a direct bus to Manaoag from the Pasay or Cubao terminal in Manila (drivers should leave by 5 AM)
Arrive in Manaoag, breakfast at a restaurant in front of the church
Attend Mass, then have religious items blessed
Climb the stairs behind the altar to touch the Virgin's mantle (panyalikip)
Offer a candle at the candle gallery, then walk the rosary garden
Lunch — bangus (milkfish) from Dagupan or a Pangasinan home-style meal
Visit the Marian museum, then shop for souvenirs and snacks
Board a bus back to Manila, or continue on toward Baguio or La Union

Weekend afternoons see heavy traffic on the buses and highway back to Manila, so it's best to go on a weekday or leave in the early afternoon if you can. Combining this with Hundred Islands or Baguio for a 2-day, 1-night trip cuts down considerably on the travel burden.
CISCO and Five Star-affiliated buses from the Pasay terminal, and Solid North buses from the Cubao terminal in Manila, run direct services to Manaoag. The trip takes about
4–5 hours
, with a one-way fare of around
. Schedules change often, so check the bus company's announcements.
If a direct departure doesn't fit your schedule, take a bus toward Dagupan, Baguio, or La Union, get off at Urdaneta or Binalonan, then continue about
20–30 minutes
by jeepney (about
) or tricycle (about
per ride).
Take the NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX expressway to the Urdaneta or Binalonan exit, then drive about
20–30 minutes
further. Without traffic, it takes about
3–4 hours
from Manila, with expressway tolls of around
one way for a car.
Several paid parking lots surround the church, with fees of about
. The lots closest to the church fill up quickly on weekend mornings, so arrive early.
Manaoag has no airport. Coming straight from Korea, Clark International Airport (CRK) is the closest, about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
away by car via the TPLEX. You can also take a Dagupan- or Baguio-bound bus from the Clark airport terminal and transfer at Urdaneta.
The church, candle gallery, museum, and rosary garden all sit within one compact area you can cover on foot. From the bus stop or a parking lot to the church, a short tricycle ride costs about
The church is open year-round, but the
November–April
dry season is best for easy travel and less rain.
March–May
gets very hot inland in Pangasinan, with midday temperatures climbing to around
, so it's better to finish your pilgrimage in the early morning.
June–October
is the rainy season, shaped by the southwest monsoon and typhoons, and heavy downpours can flood roads or delay buses.
The busiest times are Holy Week, the first Sunday of the new year, the first Sunday of every month, and October, the month of the rosary. Around feast days near the
first Sunday of October

in particular, and Marian feast days around Easter, pilgrims pour in from across the country and the roads around the church get very congested. For quiet prayer, go on a weekday morning; for festival atmosphere, time your visit to a feast day but be ready for heavy traffic.

Most visitors come on a day trip, but if you plan to attend an early Mass or combine it with nearby destinations, an overnight stay is worth considering. Simple inns and pension houses for pilgrims cluster around the church at about
a night, while Urdaneta and Dagupan, about
20–40 minutes
away by car, have chain hotels and shopping malls for a more comfortable stay at about
a night.

Pangasinan is milkfish country, and the signature dishes are grilled bangus, sour sinigang, and boneless fried bangus from neighboring Dagupan. The street in front of the church sells tupig, coconut and sticky rice grilled in banana leaf, and small, chewy Calasiao puto — both popular as pilgrimage gifts. Restaurants around the church mostly serve Filipino home cooking, and large fast-food chains are nearby too, making it easy to feed a family.
Dress modestly inside the church, avoiding sleeveless tops and short shorts. A light jacket or shawl is worth bringing along.
The line for the panyalikip is longest on weekend mornings. Weekdays or around
2–4 PM
tend to be quieter.
If you've bought a rosary or religious item, you can bring it to the blessing area after Mass to have it blessed.
Check Mass times and the feast-day schedule in advance on the church's official website or Facebook page.
Touts near the church often urge you to buy candles from them. Buying from the official vendors means your donation supports the church.
Stalls, tricycles, and parking lots take cash only, so bring plenty of small bills.
Even on a day trip, continuing on toward Baguio or Hundred Islands makes this a good first stop on a northern Luzon itinerary.
During Holy Week, the first Sunday of every month, and October feast days, the crowds are immense and pickpocketing is common. Wear your bag in front and keep your phone and wallet in hand.
Don't wander around taking photos during Mass, and avoid using flash.
The candle gallery has strong heat and smoke. If you're with children, keep clothing and hair away from the flames.
On feast days, roads around the church may be closed or jammed for hours, so allow plenty of time to get back.
Standing in line at midday in
March–May
can bring on heat exhaustion. Bring water and an umbrella for shade.
Buses may be canceled or delayed when a typhoon approaches, so check the weather forecast before you set out.
